1. Summary

  1. Background and rationale: The brown bear (Ursus arctos) is distributed in the boreal forest regions of Eastern Norway, Trøndelag, and Northern Norway, primarily along the borders with Sweden and Finland. In its reference condition the bear fulfills a complex functional role as an omnivorous apex predator and dominant scavenger. It structures the ecosystem through predation on ungulates, kleptoparasitism from wolves and lynx, and by acting as an essential seed disperser (Swenson et al. 2026). Population trends reflect habitat quality, connectivity, and anthropogenic pressures such as habitat loss and traffic mortality, in addition to policy-mandated population reduction by hunting. Norway has long-running, DNA-based monitoring of brown bears, which provides a relatively solid basis for using the species as an indicator of ecosystem condition in relevant ecosystems. The indicator is part of the Norwegian Nature Index and is documented on Naturindeksen.

  2. Methods: Estimated brown bear abundance (or an equivalent population index) is in the later years derived from the national DNA-monitoring programme and associated statistical models, not from harvest statistics. Non-lethal genetic sampling (scats, hair, and other material) is used to identify individuals; population size is estimated and reported for large-carnivore management regions (forvaltningsregioner for rovvilt, regions 5–8 in Norway). Values are normalised to a 0–1 indicator scale using reference levels (X100) defined for those management regions, with X0 representing the worst condition. Scaled values are aggregated to five geographic regions and to the national level using area weights.

  3. Interpretation: An indicator value of 1 means that the brown bear population in the reporting unit is at least as large as expected under the reference condition. Values decreasing toward zero indicate that the population index is further below the reference, reflecting negative change relative to the reference state.

  4. Results and development needs: For the current reporting period (2020-2024) the national indicator value is 0.02, with the highest value for region East (0.04) and the lowest for regions South (0.00) and West (0.00). The national indicator value has increased a little from 0.00 in 1990, with a peak in 2010 (0.03), and remained stable after 2014. For regions West and South values have been at minimum since 1990. For other regions values have varied somewhat or been stable since 2010. There are no specific development needs, except for a possible review of reference values and the scaling function.

1.2 Native language summary - Norwegian

  1. Bakgrunn og begrunnelse: Brunbjørnen (Ursus arctos) er utbredt i skog- og fjellregionene i Øst-Norge, Trøndelag og Nord-Norge. I sin referansetilstand fyller bjørnen en kompleks funksjonell rolle som en altetende toppredator og dominant åtseleter. Den strukturerer økosystemet gjennom predasjon på klovdyr, kleptoparasittisme overfor ulv og gaupe, og ved å fungere som en frøspreder (Swenson et al. 2026). Bestandsutviklingen speiler habitatkvalitet, sammenheng i landskapet og menneskelig påvirkning, blant annet tap og fragmentering av habitat, trafikkdødelighet, myndighetsbestemt bestandsregulering ved jakt. Norge har langvarig, DNA-basert overvåking av brunbjørn (Brøseth et al. 2024), som gir et relativt godt grunnlag for å bruke arten som indikator på økologisk tilstand. Indikatoren inngår i Naturindeksen og er beskrevet på Naturindeksen.

  2. Metoder: Estimert brunbjørnbestand (eller et tilsvarende bestandsindeks) bygger på det nasjonale DNA-overvåkingsprogrammet og tilhørende statistiske modeller, ikke på jaktstatistikk. Genetisk materiale (ekskrement, hår m.m.) brukes til å identifisere individer; bestandsstørrelse rapporteres for forvaltningsregioner for rovvilt. Verdiene normaliseres til en indikatorskala 0–1 med referanseverdier (X100) knyttet til disse regionene, og X0 som verste tilstand. Skalerte verdier aggregeresvidere til fem geografiske regioner og nasjonalt med arealvekter.

  3. Tolkning: En indikatorverdi på 1 betyr at brunbjørnbestanden i rapporteringsenheten er minst like stor som forventet under referansetilstanden. Verdier som nærmer seg null, viser at bestandsindekset ligger lenger under referansen og at tilstanden har utviklet seg negativt i forhold til referansen.

  4. Resultater og utviklingsbehov: For nåværende rapporteringsperiode (2020-2024) er den nasjonale indikatoren 0,02, med høyest verdi for region Øst (0,04) og lavest for regionene Sør og Vest (0,00). For hele landet har indikatorverdien økt litt fra 0,00 i 1990, med en liten topp i 2010 (0,03) og stabilt nivå siden 2014. For regionene Sør og Vest har verdien vært på minimumsnivå siden 1990. For øvrige regioner har verdiene variert noe eller vært stabile siden 2010. Det er ingen spesielle utviklingsbehov, med mulig unntak for en gjennomgang av referanseverdier og skaleringsfunksjonen.

2. About the underlying data

The primary data source for this indicator is the national programme for DNA-based monitoring of brown bears in Norway, coordinated under the large carnivore monitoring framework and reported annually (e.g. (Brøseth et al. 2024)). Prepared indicator objects (population estimates or indices with uncertainty, plus reference values) are obtained from the Naturindeks database or equivalent exports.

2.1 Spatial and temporal resolution and extent

Indicator values are available for the assessment years in Naturindeksen: 1990, 2000, 2010, 2014, 2019, and 2024. To produce indicator estimates for these years, input from the DNA-monitoring programme is combined over a short window (typically two to three years).

Brown bear abundance is estimated for large-carnivore management regions (forvaltningsregioner for rovvilt), see Rovdata and Figure 1). Indicator and reference values are stored at this management-region level (as IC units in the Naturindeksdatabase).

2.2 Sampling design

Monitoring relies on opportunistic and targeted collection of DNA samples from the field (hunters, managers, researchers, and the public), followed by genetic analysis to assign samples to individuals and sexes. Coverage is extensive but not a classical random plot design: detection depends on sample submission, field effort, and bear presence. The method is designed for capture–recapture–style inference on identified individuals rather than complete census. Biases can arise from uneven sampling intensity between areas and years, misidentified samples, and incomplete detection of individuals. Full methodological detail is given on Naturindeksen and in the annual monitoring reports (Brøseth et al. 2024).

2.3 Original units

At the monitoring stage, the core quantities are numbers of genetically identified individuals (and derived abundance or density estimates) from DNA profiles, reported nationally and by large-carnivore management regions. These are translated into indicator variables (expected values with uncertainty distributions) stored in the NI database before normalisation to 0–1.

2.4 Instructions for citing, using and accessing data

Raw genetic monitoring data is accessible in Dupont et al. (2024) and at Rovbase. Results and annual reports should be cited from the NINA monitoring publications (e.g. (Brøseth et al. 2024)). Methodological documentation for this species is linked from Naturindeksen – brunbjørn.

3. Indicator properties

3.1 Ecosystem Condition Typology Class (ECT)

The brown bear functions as an omnivorous apex predator and dominant scavenger, regulating ungulate populations, exerting competitive pressure on other large carnivores through kleptoparasitism, and contributing to seed dispersal and nutrient cycling. Through these interacting functional roles, it has the potential to exert cascading effects on vegetation composition and ecosystem structure. Hence, this indicator is considered to fall under B3 - Functional state characteristics.

3.2 Ecosystem condition characteristic

The ecosystem characteristic represented is a functionally intact large-carnivore component of boreal and montane forest ecosystems: an ecosystem where brown bear occurs at abundances consistent with the reference condition and can fulfil its ecological roles without being depressed far below sustainable levels.

3.3 Collinearities with other indicators

The indicator for brown bear may covary with other large-carnivore indicators (wolf, lynx) where distributions overlap. In a natural system this would primarily reflect shared prey availability, but for brown bear the link is weak given its largely omnivorous diet – though carrion from wolf-killed cervids can be a relevant exception. In contemporary Norway, however, population levels of all large carnivores are primarily determined by management rather than ecological dynamics.

3.4 Impact factors

Natural factors regulating brown bear population size include food availability (the primary constraint), habitat carrying capacity, and complex social interactions. In Norway, these are largely overridden by anthropogenic factors: habitat alteration and fragmentation, infrastructure and traffic mortality, and especially human–wildlife conflict, drive additional pressures. A strict zoning policy employs legal lethal removal – encompassing licensed hunting and targeted removal of conflict individuals – to prevent population establishment outside designated areas. Climate-driven changes in food availability and denning conditions may also play an increasing role.

3.5 Spatial aggregation

Following the metadata pathway Aggregate (population model, large-carnivore management region) – [Scale – Truncate] – Downscale (municipalities) – Aggregate (geographic region) – Aggregate (national level): population estimates or indices are available per large-carnivore management region. Values for each management region is normalised against X0 and X100 for that region (linear scaling with truncation to [0, 1]).

Because large-carnivore management regions and the five geographic reporting regions are two non-aligned partitions of Norway, we use municipalities (BSunits) as a common basic spatial unit. We assign the (scaled) large-carnivore management region values to each municipality belonging to that region (uniform-value assumption), hereafter referred to as downscaling. Forest area (Skog) is used as the aggregation weight because brown bear is a forest-associated species.

4. Reference condition and levels

4.1 Reference condition

The reference condition for brown bear represents the natural population state occurring in the absence of significant human influence, where population size, structure, and dynamics are regulated primarily by natural processes – including food availability (acting as the ultimate regulating factor), habitat carrying capacity, and complex social interactions and natural mortality. The population fulfills its natural functional role as an omnivorous apex predator and dominant scavenger in forest ecosystems, influencing the ecosystem through predation on ungulates (particularly moose calves) and acting as a vital seed disperser for various berry-producing shrubs and trees through endozoochory (the dispersal of seeds via ingestion and subsequent excretion), which stimulates seed germination and shapes vegetation composition. By exercising kleptoparasitism (the seizing of kills) on other carnivores such as wolves and lynx, it further influences predation rates and nutrient availability for other species, thereby structuring interactions at the community level. Population size naturally varies within dynamic ranges in response to climatic variation (affecting food phenology and denning chronology), natural disturbance regimes, and ecological interactions with both prey and competing apex predators. This condition corresponds to maximum ecological integrity of the forest ecosystem.

4.2 Reference levels

X100 is set per large-carnivore management region (IC unit in Naturindeksen), using suitable area and density within each rovviltregion and expert assessment: it represents the expected brown bear population (or equivalent index) under reference conditions in that unit.

X0 is defined as no brown bears in the unit (functional absence).

4.2.1 Spatial resolution and validity

Reference levels and indicator values apply at the scale of forvaltningsregioner for rovvilt (IC units). Aggregated results for the five Naturindeks geographic regions and for Norway are summaries of those units with area weights.

5. Uncertainties

5.1 General uncertainties

Reference levels are held fixed in this workflow (their own uncertainties are not propagated). Regional and national values are area-weighted summaries of forvaltningsregioner for rovvilt, so they inherit model uncertainty at management-region scale and any mismatch between administrative regions and ecological variation within the five Naturindeks geographic regions. Monitoring design and sample effort differ between species and regions; uneven coverage can affect the population models that enter Naturindeksen.

5.2 Reported uncertainties

The intervals in Table 2, Table 3, Figure 2, and Figure 3 are inferential: they describe uncertainty around the estimated area-weighted mean indicator for each reporting unit (a geographic region or Norway as a whole), given the statistical models used for management-region abundance in Naturindeksen.

For each management region and assessment year, Naturindeks provides a predictive distribution for the population index (on the variable scale before scaling). We draw nsim = 1000 values per region, scale each draw to the 0–1 indicator scale using the regional reference level and linear scaling, then downscale by assigning each scaled draw to every municipality in that region and aggregate with ecTools::ec_upscale(): first from municipalities (BSunits) to each NI geographic region (part), then from regions to Norway, using forest area (Skog) as the weight. The 1000 sampled_mean values per region and year describe inferential uncertainty for the forest-area-weighted mean indicator; we summarise them with the median and 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles as an approximate 95% interval, and the 25% and 75% quantiles as an approximate interquartile range.

7. Import and prepare datasets

Run the download chunk once to refresh the local export. This project’s renv environment installs NIcalc from GitHub ChloeRN/NIcalc, branch include_ReadOnly_access (see renv.lock and install_deps.R); that build defaults to the Naturindeks read-only API user, so you do not need username / password arguments here. When NINAnor/NIcalc PR #59 is merged into NINAnor/NIcalc, you can switch the renv install back to the main repo and update the lockfile. We save the RDS export under data/ so that we do not need to download the data every time we run the analysis.

Download brown bear data from Naturindeks API 
baerImport <- NIcalc::importDatasetApi(
  eco = NULL,
  indic = c("Brunbjørn"),
  year = c("1990", "2000", "2010", "2014", "2019", "2024")
)

saveRDS(baerImport, here::here("data/baerImport.rds"))

8. Spatial units

According to Naturindeks terminology, municipalities are BSunits. The eight forvaltningsregioner for rovvilt (rovvilt regions 1–8) are subsamples of BSunits and are referred to as ICunits in the import; they are the IC units for this indicator. The five Naturindeks geographic regions (east, south, west, central, north; codes E, S, W, C, N) are parts and NIunits, taken from the part field on municipality-level BSunits in the same import (see Section 9 for downscaling and aggregation). Mainland Norway is the ecosystem accounting area.

Code 
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("img/rovviltregioner.png"))

9. Analyses

This section uses the following workflow: we take variable values and reference levels from the Naturindeks import, normalise at large-carnivore management-region scale (IC unit) with linear scaling, then downscale by assigning the scaled values to the municipalities in each region and propagate uncertainty and aggregate spatially with forest-area weights using ecTools::ec_upscale(). At geographic (NI part) and national scale, uncertainties are inferential: each replicate is a forest-area-weighted mean across municipalities (then, for Norway, one draw per NI region). We use linear scaling and forest area (Skog) from the Naturindeks spatial framework as the weight.

Management-region population indices in the database are stored as predictive distributions. Reference levels per region (X0 = 0, X100 from the download) are applied before any geographic or national aggregation. We ignore uncertainty in the reference levels themselves.

Assemble import and indicator object

assembleNiObject() reshapes baerImport so that indicator observations are in one list element per assessment year, and so that underlying spatial units (BSunits) are aligned with the thematic index structure used in Naturindeks.

Assemble brown bear NI object (thematic, predefined regions) 
baerAssemble <- NIcalc::assembleNiObject(
  inputData = baerImport,
  predefNIunits = c(allArea = T, parts = T, counties = F),
  indexType = "thematic"
)

Reference levels (X0 and X100)

Before scaling, we read regional reference levels from referenceValues in the RDS export (rows with yearId == 0 or reference year name). For this indicator, X0 is zero individuals in the unit and X100 is the expert reference population index per rovvilt region (expectedValue in the reference slice).

Management-region reference levels from downloaded Naturindeks data 
refs <- baerImport$referenceValues$referenceValues |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$yearId == 0L | grepl("Referanse", .data$yearName, fixed = FALSE)) |>
  dplyr::distinct(ICunitId, ICunitName, x100 = expectedValue) |>
  dplyr::mutate(x0 = 0)
refs |>
  gt::gt()

Resample non-scaled management-region variables

For each assessment year, Naturindeks stores one value per rovvilt region as a parameterised distribution (or a custom distribution). We draw nsim = 1000 random values per region with NIcalc::sampleObsMat(). Rows with a standard distribution family use observation type tradObs; rows with only a custom distribution use customObs.

Assessment years are 1990, 2000, 2010, 2014, 2019, and 2024. The result mgmt_draws is a long table of simulated population indices (value) by ICunitId and year, not yet on the 0–1 indicator scale.

Observation types for sampleObsMat 
myYears <- as.character(c(1990, 2000, 2010, 2014, 2019, 2024))
obstype <- vector("list", length(myYears))
for (i in seq_along(myYears)) {
  obs <- baerAssemble$indicatorValues[[i]]$distributionFamilyName
  obs[!is.na(obs)] <- "tradObs"
  obs[is.na(obs)] <- "customObs"
  obstype[[i]] <- obs
}
Resample management-region variables (non-scaled) 
mgmt_draws <- tibble(ICunitId = NULL, value = NULL, year = NULL)

for (i in seq_along(myYears)) {
  myMat <- NIcalc::sampleObsMat(
    ICunitId = baerAssemble$indicatorValues[[i]]$ICunitId,
    value = baerAssemble$indicatorValues[[i]]$expectedValue,
    distrib = baerAssemble$indicatorValues[[i]]$distributionFamilyName,
    mu = baerAssemble$indicatorValues[[i]]$distParameter1,
    sig = baerAssemble$indicatorValues[[i]]$distParameter2,
    customDistribution = baerAssemble$indicatorValues[[i]]$customDistribution,
    obsType = obstype[[i]],
    nsim = 1000
  )
  ICunitIds <- row.names(myMat)
  colnames(myMat) <- paste0("s", seq_len(ncol(myMat)))
  myMat <- myMat |>
    as_tibble() |>
    add_column(ICunitId = ICunitIds, .before = 1) |>
    pivot_longer(cols = -any_of("ICunitId"), names_to = "sim_col", values_to = "value") |>
    mutate(
      sim_id = readr::parse_number(.data$sim_col),
      year = myYears[i]
    ) |>
    select(ICunitId, sim_id, value, year)

  mgmt_draws <- mgmt_draws |>
    bind_rows(myMat)
}
head(mgmt_draws) |>
  gt::gt()

Scaling to indicator values (linear)

Normalisation is done at management-region scale before any geographic or national aggregation. Each draw is joined to its regional x0 and x100, then mapped to [0, 1] with ecTools::ec_normalise() using linear increasing scaling from X0 to X100 (no upper-tail unimodal anchor).

Join reference levels and linear scaling to indicator scale 
mgmt_draws <- mgmt_draws |>
  left_join(
    refs |> mutate(ICunitId = as.character(ICunitId)),
    by = join_by(ICunitId)
  )

ind <- ec_normalise(
  variable = mgmt_draws$value,
  x0 = mgmt_draws$x0,
  x100 = mgmt_draws$x100,
  fun = "linear"
)

mgmt_draws <- mgmt_draws |> add_column(indicator = ind)

The scatter plot below (Figure 2) shows the mapping from variable to indicator for each rovvilt region (one facet per ICunitName). The figure is saved when the document is rendered.

Save normalisation diagnostic figure 
bear_norm_plot <- ec_norm_plot(mgmt_draws$value, mgmt_draws$indicator) +
  facet_wrap(. ~ mgmt_draws$ICunitName) +
  ggplot2::theme(axis.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 9))
bear_norm_plot$layers[[1]]$aes_params$size <- 3

suppressMessages(
  ggsave(
    filename = here::here("img/bear_norm_plot.png"),
    plot = bear_norm_plot,
    scale = 1.5
  )
)
Code 
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("img/bear_norm_plot.png"))

Aggregation weights (forest area by municipality)

Spatial aggregation uses forest area (Skog) on each underlying municipality in BSunits. Municipalities are linked to rovvilt regions via ICunits, and each BSunit carries a Naturindeks geographic region code (part: E, S, W, C, N). Rovvilt regions and NI parts are two non-aligned partitions of Norway, so we keep the data at municipality level once it is scaled: each municipality inherits the scaled indicator value of its rovvilt region (uniform-value assumption), and is then aggregated upward with its own forest area.

Forest area, NI part, and IC link per municipality 
mgmt_weights <- as_tibble(baerAssemble$BSunits) |>
  rename(BSunitId = id)

IC_BC_link <- baerImport$ICunits |>
  distinct(ICunitId = as.character(id), BSunitId)

mgmt_weights <- mgmt_weights |>
  left_join(IC_BC_link, by = join_by(BSunitId)) |>
  mutate(ICunitId = as.character(ICunitId))

Downscale the scaled indicator values from each rovvilt region by assigning them to every municipality in that region. The result is a long table with one row per (year, sim_id, BSunitId) carrying its rovvilt region’s indicator draw, its part, and the municipality’s Skog.

Downscale rovvilt-region draws to municipalities 
mgmt_draws <- mgmt_draws |>
  mutate(ICunitId = as.character(ICunitId))

bsunit_draws <- mgmt_draws |>
  right_join(
    mgmt_weights |> select(BSunitId, ICunitId, part, Skog),
    by = join_by(ICunitId),
    unmatched = "error",
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  )

Spatial aggregation

Aggregate from municipalities to NI geographic regions with ecTools::ec_upscale(), using Monte Carlo propagation of inferential uncertainty (one draw per municipality per replicate, forest-area-weighted mean).

Municipality to NI part MC propagation (ec_upscale) 
mc_propagated <- ecTools::ec_upscale(
  data = bsunit_draws,
  variable = indicator,
  weight = Skog,
  start_units = BSunitId,
  end_units = part,
  year = year,
  end_units_name = "part",
  n = 1000
)
saveRDS(mc_propagated, here::here("data/baer_mc_propagated_regional.rds"))

For the national indicator, propagate again from regions to Norway. Summed forest area per geographic region is used as the weight at this step.

Total forest area per NI region 
region_weights <- mgmt_weights |>
  group_by(part) |>
  summarise(forest_area = sum(.data$Skog, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
region_weights
# A tibble: 5 × 2
  part  forest_area
  <chr>       <dbl>
1 C          20568.
2 E          39436.
3 N          30469.

NI region to Norway MC propagation (ec_upscale) 
mc_propagated_for_national <- mc_propagated |>
  left_join(region_weights, by = join_by(part)) |>
  add_column(end_units = "Norway")

mc_propagated_national <- ecTools::ec_upscale(
  data = mc_propagated_for_national,
  variable = sampled_mean,
  weight = forest_area,
  start_units = part,
  end_units = end_units,
  year = year,
  end_units_name = "part",
  n = 1000
)
saveRDS(mc_propagated_national, here::here("data/baer_mc_propagated_national.rds"))

Regional and national MC draws are combined for summarisation and export.

Bind regional and national MC outputs 
mc_propagated_combined <- mc_propagated |>
  select(year, part, sampled_mean) |>
  bind_rows(mc_propagated_national)

10. Results

From the 1000 Monte Carlo replicates per region and year in mc_propagated_combined, we report the median as the point estimate and use the 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles as an approximate 95% interval for the forest-area-weighted mean indicator (inferential uncertainty, not descriptive spread between management regions). The tables (Table 2, Table 3) and time series (Figure 3) summarise regional and national (Norway) values separately.

Code 
summary_out <- mc_propagated_combined |>
  mutate(part = dplyr::recode(part, !!!baer_part_labels)) |>
  group_by(part, year) |>
  summarise(
    median = round(median(sampled_mean, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    p_025 = round(quantile(sampled_mean, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    p_25 = round(quantile(sampled_mean, probs = 0.25, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    p_75 = round(quantile(sampled_mean, probs = 0.75, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    p_975 = round(quantile(sampled_mean, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(part = factor(part, levels = baer_region_levels)) |>
  add_column(
    ECT = "B3",
    Indicator = "Brown bear abundance",
    Ecosystem = "Boreal/montane forests",
    ID = "NO_BAER_001"
  )
Code 
baer_plot_years <- as.character(c(1990, 2000, 2010, 2014, 2019, 2024))
baer_region_cols <- setNames(
  MetBrewer::met.brewer("Archambault", n = length(baer_region_levels)),
  baer_region_levels
)

plot_data <- summary_out |>
  mutate(
    year = factor(year, levels = baer_plot_years),
    series_type = if_else(part == "Norway", "National", "Region")
  )

y_hi <- max(plot_data$p_975, na.rm = TRUE)
y_max <- min(1, max(0.08, y_hi * 1.12, na.rm = TRUE))
y_breaks <- pretty(c(0, y_max), n = 6)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = year, y = median, colour = part, group = part)) +
  geom_line(
    aes(linewidth = series_type),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.18)
  ) +
  geom_pointrange(
    aes(ymin = p_025, ymax = p_975, shape = series_type),
    size = 0.8,
    linewidth = 0.45,
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.18)
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = baer_region_cols, name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c(National = 19, Region = 17),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(
    values = c(National = 1, Region = 0.55),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, y_max),
    breaks = y_breaks,
    expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.04))
  ) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.box = "vertical",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  ) +
  guides(
    colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2, override.aes = list(size = 0.7, linewidth = 0.45)),
    shape = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 0.8, linewidth = 0.45))
  ) +
  labs(y = "Indicator value", x = "")
Code 
summary_out |>
  filter(part != "Norway") |>
  arrange(part, year) |>
  unite(col = "CI_95", c(p_025, p_975), sep = " - ") |>
  unite(col = "IQR", c(p_25, p_75), sep = " - ") |>
  select(
    ECT,
    Indicator,
    ID,
    "Accounting area" = part,
    Ecosystem,
    "Closing year" = year,
    "Indicator value" = median,
    "95% CI" = CI_95,
    "50% CI" = IQR
  ) |>
  kable()
Code 
summary_out |>
  filter(part == "Norway") |>
  arrange(year) |>
  unite(col = "CI_95", c(p_025, p_975), sep = " - ") |>
  unite(col = "IQR", c(p_25, p_75), sep = " - ") |>
  select(
    ECT,
    Indicator,
    ID,
    "Accounting area" = part,
    Ecosystem,
    "Closing year" = year,
    "Indicator value" = median,
    "95% CI" = CI_95,
    "50% CI" = IQR
  ) |>
  kable()

11. Export file

Regional and national Monte Carlo draws are exported in one table (mc_propagated_combined: year, part, sampled_mean; part includes NI regions and Norway).

Export regional and national MC-propagated indicator draws 
write.csv(
  mc_propagated_combined,
  here::here("data/results_NO_BAER_001_v1.0.0.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
